title: Which of these three sets of lengths can make a triangle?
description: Three sets of lengths in kilometres, millimetres and centimetres are tested by comparing the longest side with the other two added together. Each set is tested in its own unit.
teaching_notes: One idea: the longest side is compared with the other two added together, whatever the unit, as long as all three lengths use the same unit. Watch for children who add lengths from different sets or forget the unit.

source: Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle for each of the following sets of lengths? Ten kilometres, ten kilometres and twenty five kilometres; five millimetres, ten millimetres and twenty millimetres; twelve, twenty and forty centimetres.
video_script.why: The child can compare the longest side with the other two for one set and now does it for three sets in different units.
video_script.substitution: In each set the longest side is the direct length and the other two added together are the roundabout length, in that set's own unit.
video_script.anchor: Three sets of lengths, in kilometres, millimetres and centimetres
video_script.payoff_line: No triangle exists in any of the three sets.

final_answer.spoken: no triangle exists in any of the three sets, because twenty is less than twenty five, fifteen is less than twenty and thirty two is less than forty

hold_back: No triangle exists in any of the three sets
never_show: the words no triangle exists before the answer beat
maths_rules: gaps if arcs were drawn: 25 - 20 = 5 km, 20 - 15 = 5 mm, 40 - 32 = 8 cm
video_script.design: One idea: compare the longest side with the other two added together. The three sets stay in the anchor band; the working band holds the board solution.

beats.on_screen: three cards: 10, 10, 25 km; 5, 10, 20 mm; 12, 20, 40 cm; a question mark
narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book.
Three sets of lengths are given, one in kilometres, one in millimetres and one in centimetres.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Can we say anything about a triangle for each set?

beats.on_screen: the three cards and the question mark stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a rough triangle with its longest side as the direct path in red and the other two sides as the roundabout path in yellow

marks.compare: the longest side and the other two sides are marked
marks.unit: one unit label covers all three sides

beats.colours: direct path in red, roundabout path in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Use the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='compare'/>Compare the longest side with the other two sides added together.
<bookmark mark='unit'/>All three lengths in a set use the same unit.
<bookmark mark='g1'/>Given, the first set is ten, ten and twenty five kilometres.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>The second is five, ten and twenty millimetres.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>The third is twelve, twenty and forty centimetres.

beats.on_screen: To find: whether a triangle can exist for each set
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find whether a triangle can exist for each set.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: (a) longest = 25 km; other two: 10 + 10 = 20 km; 25 > 20

marks.others: 10 and 10 are added to 20 in yellow

beats.colours: direct length in red, roundabout length in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='longest'/>Step one, in the first set the longest side is twenty five kilometres.
<bookmark mark='others'/>The other two add to ten plus ten, which is twenty.
<bookmark mark='compare'/>Twenty five is greater than twenty, so the direct length is longer.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: (b) longest = 20 mm; other two: 5 + 10 = 15 mm; 20 > 15

marks.others: 5 and 10 are added to 15 in yellow

beats.colours: direct length in red, roundabout length in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='longest'/>Step two, in the second set the longest side is twenty millimetres.
<bookmark mark='others'/>The other two add to five plus ten, which is fifteen.
<bookmark mark='compare'/>Twenty is greater than fifteen, so the direct length is longer.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: (c) longest = 40 cm; other two: 12 + 20 = 32 cm; 40 > 32

marks.others: 12 and 20 are added to 32 in yellow

beats.colours: direct length in red, roundabout length in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='longest'/>Step three, in the third set the longest side is forty centimetres.
<bookmark mark='others'/>The other two add to twelve plus twenty, which is thirty two.
<bookmark mark='compare'/>Forty is greater than thirty two, so the direct length is longer.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check: arcs would leave gaps of 5 km, 5 mm and 8 cm

marks.gaps: three gaps are shown beside the three sets

narration: <bookmark mark='gaps'/>Step four, check with arcs.
They would leave gaps of five kilometres, five millimetres and eight centimetres.
The arcs would not meet in any set.

beats.on_screen: Answer: No triangle exists in any of the three sets: 20 < 25, 15 < 20, 32 < 40
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>No triangle exists in any of the three sets.
